title: Personal hygiene, skin, mouth, eye and nail care
blurb: Help people wash, dress and care for mouth, skin, eyes and nails while promoting independence, and know when to refer.
question: Mrs Lowe, 81, is recovering from pneumonia and wants to go home. She can wash her face and upper body slowly but tires easily. A healthcare support worker offers to give her a full bed bath to save time. What should the nurse advise?

teach.h: Hygiene is a fundamental of care
teach.body: The NMC Code lists keeping people 'in clean and hygienic conditions' among the fundamentals of care that you must deliver effectively. Personal care is also an assessment opportunity: you see skin, mouth, feet, mobility, mood and independence. In plain English: help people stay clean and comfortable in the way they choose, let them do what they can, and use the time to spot problems early.
teach.cite: NMC Code (2015, updated 2018) clause 1.2 and note

steps.label: Ask and plan
steps.sub: Preferences, products, timing, culture, gender of carer

steps.label: Privacy
steps.sub: Close curtains fully, cover what is not being washed

steps.label:
They do
what they can
steps.sub: Set up within reach; you help with the rest

teach.caption: NICE NG249 (falls) encourages people in hospital to get out of bed, get dressed and stay active.

head: Need
What to do
rows: Brush at least twice a day with fluoride toothpaste
Clean daily, remove food debris, remove overnight
Use the person's choice of toothbrush and denture cleaner
Use high-fluoride toothpaste or mouthwash daily as prescribed
Mouth care needs in the care plan; dentures marked with consent
teach.caption: NICE NG48 Oral health for adults in care homes (2016) recs 1.2.1–1.2.4 and 1.3.1; its daily routine follows the national Delivering better oral health toolkit. NICE CG103 also asks staff to check dentures fit properly, as poor fit affects nutrition.

teach.h: Mouth care when someone cannot manage
teach.body: People who are drowsy, nil by mouth, receiving oxygen or dying quickly develop a dry, coated mouth and cracked lips, which is painful and raises infection risk. Use a soft small toothbrush and gentle technique, keep lips moist, and check the mouth for problems such as white patches that wipe off to leave a red base (possible oral thrush), ulcers or bleeding gums, and report them so they can be treated. NICE NG31 recommends frequent mouth and lip care in the last days of life.

teach.h: Scenario: Mrs Lowe preparing for home
teach.body: A full bed bath would be quicker but would take away the independence Mrs Lowe needs to get home. The nurse advises the support worker to set her up at the sink or bedside with everything in reach, let her wash her face and upper body at her own pace, then help with her back, legs and feet. They check her heels and sacrum during the wash, encourage her to dress in her own clothes and record what she managed, so the discharge plan reflects her real ability.

teach.h: Skin and nail findings: act or refer?

children.edge: New rash after a new medicine
children.label: Withhold and tell prescriber
Refer feet to podiatry
children.sub: Foot protection service gives nail care

teach.caption: NICE NG19: people with diabetes at moderate or high foot risk (for example neuropathy) are referred to the podiatry-led foot protection service, which provides skin and nail care.

items: Wash hands and explain; use clean technique.
Use a fresh swab for each eye so infection is not carried from one eye to the other.
Report redness, discharge, pain or a change in vision.
Make sure glasses are clean and worn, and that hearing aids work (NICE CG103: sensory aids help prevent delirium).

teach.text: Doing everything for a person is not always the kind option. Promoting independence (letting someone wash what they can, dress in their own clothes, walk to the bathroom) preserves dignity and function and supports discharge. The exception is when doing it would harm them, which is why you assess first.

items: Hygiene is a fundamental of care (Code 1.2); respect preferences and privacy.
Promote independence: set up, let the person do what they can, help with the rest.
Natural teeth: brush at least twice daily with fluoride toothpaste; dentures cleaned daily and out overnight (NG48).
Report oral problems such as thrush; frequent mouth and lip care for people who are dying (NG31).
New rash after a new drug: withhold and tell the prescriber. Diabetic foot risk: refer to podiatry (NG19).

summary: You can now give personal care that promotes independence and dignity, deliver daily mouth and denture care to NICE NG48, and recognise skin, mouth and foot findings that need reporting or referral.

A.q: Mr Barton, 79, has full upper and lower dentures and asks what to do with them at night while in hospital. What is the best advice?
options: Keep them in overnight so that his gums do not shrink
Clean them and store them dry in a tissue by the bed
Soak them in hot water overnight to sterilise them
Remove, clean and store them in a labelled pot
A.why: Daily denture care in NICE NG48 rec 1.3.1 (written for care homes, following the national Delivering better oral health toolkit) includes cleaning, removing food debris and removing dentures overnight. A labelled pot prevents loss or damage.

whyNot.0: NG48 includes removing dentures overnight in daily denture care, so wearing them all night is not advised.
whyNot.1: Dentures wrapped in tissue are easily thrown away or damaged.
whyNot.2: Hot water can warp dentures and does not replace cleaning.

A.q: How often does NICE NG48 recommend that a person's natural teeth are brushed with fluoride toothpaste?
options: Once a day
After every meal
At least twice a day
Three times each week
A.why: NICE NG48 rec 1.3.1: brush natural teeth at least twice a day with fluoride toothpaste.

whyNot.0: Once a day is below the NG48 minimum.
whyNot.1: After every meal is not the NG48 wording; the minimum is twice daily.
whyNot.3: Three times a week falls well below the daily standard.

A.q: Mr Quinn, 74, takes apixaban for atrial fibrillation. He usually wet shaves with a blade razor and asks for help to shave in hospital. What is most appropriate?
options: Use an electric razor to reduce the risk of bleeding
Use a new blade razor and press firmly for a close shave
Advise him not to shave until the apixaban is stopped
Use a blade razor and apply pressure to any small cuts
A.why: Anticoagulants increase bleeding from small cuts, so an electric razor is the safer way to support his usual grooming.

whyNot.1: Firm pressure with a blade increases the risk of cuts and bleeding.
whyNot.2: Stopping grooming is unnecessary and undermines dignity; a safer method exists.
whyNot.3: Planning to manage cuts accepts an avoidable bleeding risk.

B.q: Mr Ward, 80, is nil by mouth and drowsy. During mouth care the nurse sees white patches on his tongue that wipe off, leaving a red base. What should the nurse do?
options: Scrape off the patches firmly with a foam stick
Report probable oral thrush so it can be treated
Record it as normal coating from being nil by mouth
Rinse his mouth with an alcohol-based mouthwash
B.why: White patches that wipe off to leave a red base suggest oral candidiasis (thrush). Report it so treatment can be prescribed, and continue gentle mouth care.

whyNot.0: Firm scraping damages the mucosa and does not treat the infection.
whyNot.2: Calling it normal coating misses a treatable infection.
whyNot.3: Alcohol-based products dry and sting an already sore mouth.

B.q: Mrs Okafor, 66, develops a new itchy, raised red rash on her trunk two days after starting an antibiotic. Her observations are normal and she has no swelling or wheeze. What should the nurse do?
options: Apply a moisturiser and continue the antibiotic as prescribed
Give the next dose and review the rash at the end of the course
Withhold the next dose and inform the prescriber promptly
Ask her to wash with a different soap and reassess tomorrow
B.why: A new rash after a new drug may be an adverse reaction. Withhold the next dose, inform the prescriber, record it and report via Yellow Card if a suspected reaction (RPS/RCN 2019; MHRA).

whyNot.0: Continuing risks a worsening reaction without medical review.
whyNot.1: Waiting until the end of the course ignores a possible drug reaction.
whyNot.3: A soap change does not address a probable drug reaction.

B.q: Mrs Hall, 79, has type 2 diabetes and reduced sensation in both feet. Her toenails are long and thickened, and she asks the nurse to cut them. What is most appropriate?
options: Cut them straight across after soaking her feet
File them down instead of cutting to avoid any injury
Ask her family to bring in her own clippers to use
Explain the risk and refer her to podiatry
B.why: Neuropathy places her at least at moderate foot risk; NICE NG19 refers such people to the podiatry-led foot protection service, which provides nail care.

whyNot.0: Cutting thickened nails on a neuropathic foot risks unnoticed injury and ulceration.
whyNot.1: Filing still risks skin damage she may not feel; specialist care is needed.
whyNot.2: Her own clippers do not reduce the risk; the issue is the specialist skill needed.

C.q: Mr Ahmed, 72, is admitted with a stroke and has an unsafe swallow. His lips are cracked and his tongue is dry and coated. Which plan is most appropriate?
options: Gentle mouth care with a soft brush and lip balm
Small sips of water to moisten his mouth every hour
Mouth care once daily with a foam stick and mouthwash
Leave mouth care until his swallow has been reassessed
C.why: People who are nil by mouth still need regular, gentle mouth care with a soft brush and lip moisturiser to prevent soreness and infection (NG48 principles).

whyNot.1: Oral fluids are unsafe with an unsafe swallow.
whyNot.2: Once daily is too infrequent for a dry, coated mouth; a soft brush cleans better.
whyNot.3: Delaying mouth care allows the mouth to deteriorate further.

C.q: Mrs Grant, 84, has dementia and refuses to let staff remove her dentures at night, becoming distressed. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Remove them while she sleeps to prevent any argument
Explore why, try again later and record her mouth care plan
Leave them in permanently and stop offering mouth care
Ask two staff to hold her hands while the dentures are removed
C.why: NG48 rec 1.3.4 expects staff to know how to respond if a resident does not want mouth care or to have her dentures removed. A person-centred response explores her reasons, tries again at a better time and records the agreed approach in her mouth care plan (rec 1.2.4).

whyNot.0: Removing them covertly while she sleeps disregards her wishes and could frighten her.
whyNot.2: Stopping mouth care risks oral disease; the aim is to find an approach she accepts.
whyNot.3: Holding her is a restrictive intervention that is disproportionate here.

C.q: Mr Edwards, 77, is independent at home but on the ward has had all personal care done for him for a week. He now says he 'can't manage' washing. What is the most appropriate nursing response?
options: Continue full personal care as he now feels unable to manage
Arrange a care package for washing before he is discharged
Set him up to do what he can and plan to increase it daily
Withdraw help so that he rebuilds confidence on his own
C.why: Promoting independence supports function and discharge; NG249 encourages people in hospital to get up, dressed and active. Grade the help and record progress.

whyNot.0: Continuing to do everything worsens deconditioning and dependence.
whyNot.1: A care package may be unnecessary if his ability is rebuilt on the ward.
whyNot.3: Withdrawing help suddenly is unsafe and may knock his confidence further.

reteach.title: Set up, step back, look closely
reteach.question: Personal care has three jobs: cleanliness, independence and assessment. How can one wash do all three?

blocks.body: Cleanliness: the person ends up clean and comfortable in the way they like. Independence: you set things up and step back so they do as much as safely possible. Assessment: while they wash you look at skin, pressure areas, feet and mouth and notice breathlessness, pain or low mood. Recording what you found and what they managed turns a routine task into nursing care.

blocks.text: A finding you notice but do not record or report does not help the person: a new rash, a sore mouth or a red heel needs to reach the right person.

explain.body: Ask about preferences, ensure privacy, set the person up with what they need and let them do what they can; help with the rest. Encourage dressing in own clothes and staying active (NG249).

test.q: Which approach best promotes independence during a wash?
options: Wash the person fully to save their energy
Set things up so they wash what they can
Leave them unsupervised with a bowl of water
Wait until a relative can help them
test.why: Setting up and letting the person do what they can, with help for the rest, promotes independence safely.

whyNot.0: Doing everything removes the chance to maintain function.
whyNot.2: Leaving them alone without assessment may be unsafe.
whyNot.3: Care should not be delayed for family; it is the nurse's role.

explain.body: Brush natural teeth at least twice daily with fluoride toothpaste. Clean dentures daily and remove them overnight. Use the person's choice of products. Record mouth care needs in the care plan.

test.q: According to NICE NG48, what should happen to dentures overnight?
options: They are worn to keep their shape
They are soaked in boiling water
They are left in a dry tissue
They are removed after cleaning
test.why: NG48 includes removing dentures overnight as part of daily denture care.

whyNot.0: Wearing them overnight is not advised.
whyNot.2: Tissue-wrapped dentures are easily lost or damaged.

explain.body: Check the skin at every wash: pressure areas, folds, moisture damage, rashes. A new rash after a new medicine may be an adverse drug reaction: withhold the next dose, inform the prescriber, record it.

test.q: A new rash appears a day after starting a new medicine. Which first action is best?
options: Withhold and inform the prescriber
Apply a steroid cream to the rash
Continue it and recheck next week
Change her soap and washing products
test.why: A possible drug reaction needs the next dose withheld and prompt review by the prescriber.

whyNot.1: A steroid cream needs a prescription and does not address the cause.
whyNot.2: Waiting a week risks a worsening reaction.
whyNot.3: Changing products ignores the likely cause.

explain.body: People with diabetes and neuropathy or poor circulation are at moderate or high foot risk. NICE NG19 refers them to the podiatry-led foot protection service, which gives advice on and provides skin and nail care.

test.q: Who should provide nail care for a person with diabetes and neuropathy?
options: The podiatry foot protection service
Any registered nurse on the ward team
A healthcare support worker
The person's family at home
test.why: NICE NG19: people at moderate or high risk are referred to the foot protection service, which provides skin and nail care.

whyNot.1: Ward nurses should refer rather than cut high-risk nails.
whyNot.2: Support workers should not cut nails on a neuropathic foot.
whyNot.3: Family members lack the specialist skills needed for a high-risk foot.
